response.answer_text: AUG differs from the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA in that AUG both specifies the amino acid methionine and serves as the start codon that initiates translation [ev_004] [ev_006]. The reading frame is set by the AUG start codon near the 5' end of the mRNA, and the mRNA is then read in groups of three [ev_004] [ev_006]. In contrast, three of the 64 codons are stop codons, which terminate protein synthesis and release the polypeptide from the translation machinery [ev_004] [ev_006]. Stop codons are called nonsense codons, and they do not instruct the addition of an amino acid to the chain [ev_004] [ev_007]. When the ribosome encounters a stop codon, the growing polypeptide is released and the ribosome subunits dissociate and leave the mRNA [ev_002]. Termination occurs when a nonsense codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is encountered; upon aligning with the A site, these codons are recognized by protein release factors that resemble tRNAs [ev_007] [ev_001]. The releasing factors instruct peptidyl transferase to add a water molecule to the carboxyl end of the P-site amino acid, which forces that amino acid to detach from its tRNA, and the newly made protein is released [ev_001]. Entry of a release factor into the A site terminates translation and the components dissociate [ev_007]. The small and large ribosomal subunits then dissociate from the mRNA and from each other [ev_001].
